case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 11 U.S.C. § 544(b)(1), together with Bankruptcy Code § 106(a)’s waiver of sovereign immunity, lets a bankruptcy trustee use state fraudulent-transfer law to claw back tax payments made to the United States even when no real-world creditor could sue the United States outside bankruptcy because of sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. § 544(b)(1) (trustee’s strong-arm power to avoid transfers voidable by an actual unsecured creditor under applicable law) and 11 U.S.C. § 106(a) (waiver of sovereign immunity “with respect to” enumerated Bankruptcy Code provisions, including § 544).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 544(b)(1) incorporates an “actual creditor” requirement: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if there exists at least one unsecured creditor who, outside bankruptcy, could bring the same state-law fraudulent-transfer action against the same transferee. Because sovereign immunity would bar any creditor from suing the United States under state law to unwind tax payments, the trustee likewise cannot do so via § 544(b)(1). In the government’s view, § 106(a)’s waiver does not eliminate § 544(b)(1)’s embedded limitation (that the transfer must be ‘voidable … by a creditor’) and should not be read to create a broader avoidance right against the federal government than any creditor would have in nonbankruptcy litigation.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Miller (and supporting amici) argue that § 106(a) broadly and unambiguously waives federal sovereign immunity ‘with respect to’ § 544, so the United States cannot defeat a trustee’s § 544(b)(1) action by invoking sovereign immunity as a defense. On this view, § 544(b)(1)’s requirement is satisfied so long as there is a creditor holding an allowable claim who could void the transfer under ‘applicable law’ in the sense that the transfer is fraudulent under state law; sovereign immunity is not part of the state-law merits of voidability but a separate jurisdictional/defense barrier that Congress removed in bankruptcy through § 106(a). Respondent also points to Congress’s historical intent to enact a durable, broad bankruptcy waiver (especially through the 1994 amendments responding to prior Supreme Court waiver cases), and contends the government’s narrowing construction improperly ‘imports’ immunity back into § 544 despite § 106(a)’s text.
key_precedents: Ohio Adjutant General’s Department v. FLRA, 598 U.S. 449 (2023)
Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp., 513 U.S. 374 (1995)
United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992)
Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance, 492 U.S. 96 (1989)
Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44 (1996)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 106(a) expressly waives immunity “with respect to” § 544 and we should avoid reading that waiver into near-irrelevance. But as Justice Kagan underscores, § 544(b)(1) is derivative by design: it authorizes avoidance only if the transfer is “voidable … by a creditor” under applicable law, and sovereign immunity is part of the real-world legal landscape determining whether any creditor has that cause of action against this transferee. Under Nordic Village’s clear-statement rule (as Justice Alito and Justice Thomas emphasize), we should not treat § 106(a)’s general “with respect to” language as silently transforming § 544(b)(1) into a bankruptcy-only avoidance right against the United States that no creditor could assert outside bankruptcy. A narrow holding preserves institutional legitimacy: § 106(a) removes immunity where § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor prerequisite is otherwise satisfied, but it does not displace that prerequisite when the only putative creditor claim would be jurisdictionally barred absent some separate, unmistakable waiver.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 106(a)’s waiver would be rendered hollow if § 544(b)(1)’s “voidable … by a creditor” language simply smuggled immunity back in. But textually, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, § 544(b)(1) makes the trustee’s power derivative and conditional on the existence of an actual creditor who, under “applicable law,” could void the transfer against the same transferee; if sovereign immunity forecloses any such suit against the United States, that statutory condition is unsatisfied rather than defeated by an avoidable “defense.” Nordic Village and Hoffman reinforce that we cannot treat § 106(a)’s “with respect to” as an unmistakably clear authorization to create a bankruptcy-only avoidance right broader than any creditor possesses outside bankruptcy. Section 106(a) still does real work—waiving immunity in § 544 actions when a qualifying creditor exists—but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s embedded actual-creditor limitation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is that the 1994 amendment to § 106(a) was meant to provide the clarity Hoffman and Nordic Village demanded, and that our reading risks making the waiver pointless in the very setting where it matters. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 544(b)(1) is derivative by its own terms: the trustee may avoid only a transfer that is actually “voidable … by a creditor” under applicable law, which presupposes a real creditor with a viable cause of action against the same transferee in the nonbankruptcy world. If sovereign immunity forecloses every creditor’s ability to obtain that relief against the United States, then the statutory predicate fails; § 106(a) can waive immunity “with respect to” § 544 without rewriting § 544(b)(1) into a bankruptcy-only avoidance power, and Nordic Village counsels against inferring such a consequential expansion from general waiver language. On a practical-consequences view, respondent’s construction would expose federal payments to broad state-law avoidance theories without an unmistakably clear congressional directive, a result our immunity precedents caution us to avoid.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the strongest point that § 544(b)(1) is derivative and demands a real-world creditor who could sue the same transferee, so sovereign immunity means the “voidable … by a creditor” condition fails. But that framing effectively bakes a federal sovereign-immunity bar into the meaning of “voidable” under “applicable law,” even though immunity is a separate, federal jurisdictional defense that Congress expressly removed “with respect to” § 544 in § 106(a); reading § 544(b)(1) to reintroduce that defense through the creditor-reference makes § 106(a)’s specific listing of § 544 largely pointless where the United States is the transferee. Nordic Village and Hoffman require clarity for waivers, and the 1994 amendments supplied it by naming § 544; I cannot, consistent with bankruptcy’s equitable-distribution aims and the real-world harms to ordinary creditors, treat § 106(a) as doing only a sliver of work when Congress spoke directly. While Justice Alito worries about expansive exposure, that policy concern cannot override the statute Congress wrote, and any remaining limits come from the incorporated state-law cause of action itself, not a resurrected immunity bar.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that § 106(a)’s express waiver would do little work if § 544(b)(1)’s “voidable … by a creditor” clause is read to let sovereign immunity defeat every action against the United States. But as the Chief Justice stresses, § 544(b)(1) is textually structured as a derivative power with an incorporated predicate—there must exist an actual creditor who can avoid the transfer under “applicable law”—and sovereign immunity goes to whether that real-world cause of action exists at all, not merely to a waivable litigation defense. The clear-statement line (Nordic Village, Hoffman, and as Justice Alito notes Cooper/Lac du Flambeau’s strict construction) makes me unwilling to treat § 106(a)’s “with respect to” language as silently transforming § 544(b) into a bankruptcy-only avoidance right against the sovereign that no creditor possesses outside bankruptcy. I therefore stay with petitioner: § 106(a) removes the Government’s immunity where the trustee otherwise satisfies § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor requirement, but it does not erase that requirement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s principal claim—that sovereign immunity is merely a federal defense that § 106(a) removes “with respect to” § 544—has force only if § 544(b)(1)’s “voidable … by a creditor” language does not itself require a real-world creditor capable of obtaining that relief against the same transferee. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 544(b)(1) is expressly derivative: it authorizes the trustee to act only when some actual unsecured creditor has a viable cause of action under “applicable law,” and sovereign immunity bears directly on whether any creditor can sue the United States at all. Reading § 106(a) to erase that embedded limitation would effectively transform § 544(b)(1) into a bankruptcy-only avoidance right against the sovereign—an expansion we cannot infer from “with respect to” given the strict clear-statement rule in Nordic Village and its successors. § 106(a) still does work on our reading by removing immunity where a qualifying creditor exists; it just does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s predicate.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that § 106(a)’s waiver should not be rendered a practical nullity by letting immunity reenter through § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-reference. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, § 544(b)(1) is derivative by design: the trustee’s authority exists only if an actual unsecured creditor could avoid the transfer against the same transferee under applicable law in the real world, and sovereign immunity is part of that real-world legal landscape determining whether any creditor has a viable cause of action against the United States. Reading § 106(a)’s “with respect to” language to erase that embedded prerequisite would not just remove a defense; it would silently transform § 544 into a bankruptcy-only avoidance power against the sovereign—an expansion Nordic Village and related clear-statement cases counsel us not to infer without unmistakable textual direction. On an institutionalist, precedent-respecting approach, the narrower construction preserves § 544(b)(1)’s longstanding structure while still giving § 106(a) meaningful work when a qualifying creditor exists.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is that Congress enacted § 106(a) to supply the clear statement Hoffman and Nordic Village demanded, and we should not let § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-reference function as a backdoor immunity. But I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that § 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: it authorizes avoidance only of transfers “voidable … by a creditor” under “applicable law,” which incorporates the real-world ability of some creditor to sue the same transferee; sovereign immunity can mean that predicate never exists rather than merely supplying a waivable defense. Reading § 106(a)’s “with respect to” language to erase § 544(b)(1)’s embedded actual-creditor condition would silently convert a state-law-derivative power into a bankruptcy-only avoidance right against the United States, a significant expansion that Nordic Village counsels us not to infer absent unmistakable textual direction. On that understanding, § 106(a) still does work—removing immunity where a qualifying creditor exists—without rewriting § 544(b)(1)’s substantive prerequisite.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that § 106(a)’s express waiver should not be reduced to a nullity; if the Government could always evade § 544(b)(1) via immunity, listing § 544 in § 106(a) would do little work in the very cases where the sovereign is the transferee. But I remain persuaded by Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that § 544(b)(1) is structurally derivative and makes an actual, real-world creditor’s ability to avoid the transfer a substantive predicate—not merely a defense question—and sovereign immunity can determine whether any such creditor exists. Nordic Village and FAA v. Cooper (as the Chief notes) reinforce that we should not treat “with respect to” as silently converting a state-law-derivative trustee power into a bankruptcy-only avoidance right against the United States with significant fiscal consequences absent an unmistakable statement. On my pragmatic, procedure-focused view, the cleaner, narrower path is to read § 106(a) as removing immunity in properly constituted § 544 actions while leaving intact § 544(b)(1)’s requirement that some creditor could sue the same transferee outside bankruptcy.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) by its terms authorizes avoidance only of a transfer that is “voidable … by a creditor” under “applicable law,” which requires the existence of an actual unsecured creditor who could bring the same state-law action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy. Although § 106(a) waives sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, that waiver is best read as removing immunity as a defense in otherwise-authorized § 544 actions, not as expanding § 544(b)(1)’s substantive “actual creditor” prerequisite to create an avoidance right no creditor possesses in the real world. Under the clear-statement rule for waivers of sovereign immunity, any plausible reading that preserves immunity (or, here, preserves embedded statutory limits that prevent an end-run around immunity) must be adopted absent unmistakably clear text to the contrary. See United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992); FAA v. Cooper, 566 U.S. 284 (2012); Lac du Flambeau Band v. Coughlin, 599 U.S. 382 (2023).

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually limited to transfers “voidable … by a creditor,” which requires an actual unsecured creditor who could bring the same avoidance action against the same transferee under “applicable law” outside bankruptcy; if sovereign immunity would bar every such creditor from suing the United States, then the transfer is not “voidable … by a creditor” as § 544(b)(1) demands. Section 106(a) waives sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s incorporated actual-creditor limitation or create a freestanding cause of action broader than any creditor possesses. This reading accords with the rule that waivers of federal sovereign immunity must be unequivocally expressed and strictly construed, as emphasized in Nordic Village and Hoffman. Because Congress did not clearly state that § 106(a) eliminates § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor requirement as applied to the United States, the trustee’s state-law fraudulent-transfer claim cannot proceed.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually limited to transfers that are "voidable under applicable law by a creditor," which presupposes an actual unsecured creditor who could bring the same avoidance action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy; if sovereign immunity would defeat every such creditor’s state-law suit against the United States, the trustee cannot satisfy that embedded requirement. Section 106(a) waives the Government’s immunity "with respect to" § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s substantive predicate or create a broader avoidance right than any real creditor possesses—especially given the clear-statement rule that waivers are "construed strictly in favor of the sovereign." Reading § 106(a) to dispense with the actual-creditor limitation would effectively transform § 544(b)(1) into a freestanding federal cause of action against the United States, a significant expansion Congress did not unmistakably enact. That restrained reading accords with Nordic Village’s insistence on demanding clarity in sovereign-immunity waivers and avoids disruptive practical consequences for federal fiscal administration.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 106(a) unequivocally waives federal sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, and reading § 544(b)(1)’s “actual creditor” language to reintroduce immunity would undermine the very remedial scheme Congress strengthened in the 1994 amendments after Hoffman and Nordic Village demanded clearer waivers. The trustee still must identify an allowable unsecured creditor and prove the transfer is “voidable … under applicable law,” but sovereign immunity is not an element of state-law voidability; it is a separate federal defense Congress removed in bankruptcy through § 106(a). This construction fits the clear-statement rule from Nordic Village without treating Congress’s explicit waiver as an empty gesture, and it better serves bankruptcy’s equitable function of maximizing the estate for all creditors, including vulnerable ones harmed by fraudulent transfers.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually conditional: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if it is “voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim,” which naturally imports the real-world ability of at least one actual creditor to bring that same cause of action against the same transferee. Section 106(a) unquestionably waives the United States’ sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s incorporated actual-creditor limitation or transform state law into something “voidable … by a creditor” when sovereign immunity would bar every creditor’s suit outside bankruptcy. Given the clear-statement rule that waivers must be “unequivocally expressed” and are construed strictly in the sovereign’s favor, reading § 106(a) to eliminate § 544(b)(1)’s embedded predicate goes beyond what Congress said, even after the 1994 amendments responding to Hoffman and Nordic Village. That narrower construction is also more workable and coherent because it preserves § 544(b)(1)’s derivative design rather than creating a bankruptcy-only federal avoidance right pegged to state law but unavailable to any actual creditor.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) authorizes avoidance only of a transfer “voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim,” which, by its plain terms, requires an actual creditor who could bring the same action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy; where sovereign immunity would defeat any such creditor’s state-law suit against the United States, the transfer is not “voidable … by a creditor.” Section 106(a) waives sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s embedded actual-creditor limitation or create a new federal cause of action untethered from what “applicable law” makes voidable by a creditor. Given the clear-statement rule that waivers of sovereign immunity must be “unequivocally expressed” and are construed strictly in favor of the sovereign, any plausible reading that preserves immunity in this setting must prevail. Nordic Village underscores that point and cautions against inferring a broader monetary avoidance remedy against the United States absent unmistakable statutory text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) by its text authorizes avoidance only of a transfer that is “voidable … by a creditor” under applicable law, which historically has required an actual unsecured creditor who could bring the same action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy; if sovereign immunity would bar any such creditor from suing the United States, the trustee cannot satisfy § 544(b)(1)’s embedded actual-creditor requirement. Section 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 should be read to remove the United States’ immunity as a bankruptcy defendant where the trustee otherwise has a valid § 544(b)(1) cause of action, not to expand § 544(b)(1) into a new, broader avoidance right untethered to any real creditor’s ability to sue. Under the clear-statement rule, waivers must be “unequivocally expressed” and construed strictly in favor of the sovereign; where a plausible reading preserves immunity’s practical effect in this context, that reading controls. See United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30, 34 (1992).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) authorizes avoidance only of a transfer “voidable under applicable law by a creditor holding an unsecured claim,” which, on its face, requires an actual creditor who could bring the same action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy; sovereign immunity means no such creditor exists for suits against the United States. Section 106(a) waives immunity “with respect to” § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s embedded actual-creditor predicate or transform state-law ‘voidability’ into something that exists even when no creditor could sue the sovereign in the real world. Under the clear-statement rule, waivers of federal sovereign immunity are strictly construed and courts must adopt a plausible immunity-preserving interpretation absent unequivocal text to the contrary. Reading § 106(a) to eliminate § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor limitation would create a broader avoidance right against the United States than any creditor possesses under “applicable law,” a result not clearly expressed in the statutory text.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually limited to transfers that are “voidable … by a creditor” under “applicable law,” which imports an actual-creditor requirement: there must exist at least one unsecured creditor who could bring the same state-law action against the same transferee outside bankruptcy. Although § 106(a) unequivocally waives sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, that waiver removes the United States’ immunity as a defendant in bankruptcy court; it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s embedded predicate that the cause of action be one a real creditor could assert in the first place. Reading § 106(a) to dispense with the actual-creditor limitation would expand § 544 beyond its established derivative design and would conflict with the clear-statement rule that waivers are construed strictly in the sovereign’s favor, as emphasized in Nordic Village. The practical consequence of respondent’s reading would be to create a uniquely bankruptcy-only fraudulent-transfer cause of action against the federal government untethered from any nonbankruptcy creditor right, a significant alteration Congress did not clearly state in § 544’s text.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 11 U.S.C. § 544(b)(1) permits a bankruptcy trustee to use state fraudulent-transfer law to avoid a debtor’s tax payments to the United States when no real-world creditor could sue the United States outside bankruptcy because of federal sovereign immunity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 11 U.S.C. §§ 544(b)(1) and 106(a) (Bankruptcy Code—trustee’s “strong-arm”/derivative avoidance power and the federal government’s waiver of sovereign immunity “with respect to” specified Bankruptcy Code sections, including § 544).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 544(b)(1) is derivative: a trustee may avoid a transfer only if an actual unsecured creditor could have avoided it under “applicable law” outside bankruptcy. Because sovereign immunity would bar any creditor’s state-law fraudulent-transfer suit against the United States outside bankruptcy, there is no qualifying creditor and thus no § 544(b)(1) avoidance action against the government. In the government’s view, § 106(a)’s waiver does not supply the missing ‘actual creditor’ predicate under § 544(b)(1); it merely removes a jurisdictional/immunity defense once the trustee otherwise satisfies § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-based condition.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Miller argues that § 106(a) broadly and unambiguously waives federal sovereign immunity ‘with respect to’ § 544, so trustees may bring § 544(b)(1) actions against the United States to the same extent they may bring them against private transferees. On this view, reading sovereign immunity back into § 544(b)(1) would contradict Congress’s express waiver and undermine bankruptcy’s core policy of equitable asset recovery; the ‘actual creditor’ requirement is satisfied so long as there exists a creditor with a viable state-law fraudulent-transfer claim absent the special obstacle of federal sovereign immunity (which § 106(a) removes in bankruptcy).
key_precedents: Lebron v. National Railroad Passenger Corp., 513 U.S. 374 (1995)
Ohio Adjutant General’s Department v. FLRA, 598 U.S. 449 (2023)
United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992)
Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance, 492 U.S. 96 (1989)
Seminole Tribe of Florida v. Florida, 517 U.S. 44 (1996)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that § 106(a)’s express waiver “with respect to” § 544 should not be rendered functionally meaningless in the very setting where immunity is predictably invoked; that is the best argument on the other side. But as Justice Kagan explains, § 544(b)(1) is not merely an “immunity obstacle”—it defines the trustee’s avoiding power by incorporating an actual creditor’s nonbankruptcy rights, so if sovereign immunity means no creditor “may avoid” the transfer under applicable law, the statutory predicate never arises in the first place. Nordic Village’s strict-construction rule for waivers (emphasized by Justice Alito and others) reinforces that we should not treat § 106(a) as silently transforming “a creditor … may avoid” into a hypothetical-creditor construct, which would expand substantive exposure beyond what any real creditor could assert outside bankruptcy. A narrow holding—no qualifying triggering creditor here, while § 106(a) still does work where such a creditor exists—best preserves text, precedent, and institutional legitimacy without resolving more than necessary.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “hollow waiver” point deserves a straight answer: § 106(a) can do substantial work without rewriting § 544(b)(1)’s triggering condition, because it removes immunity in § 544 actions where an actual creditor exists who “may avoid” under applicable law, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain. But where sovereign immunity means no unsecured creditor can bring the incorporated state-law action against the United States outside bankruptcy, § 544(b)(1)’s derivative predicate is not met, and § 106(a)’s general phrase “with respect to” cannot be stretched to supply a missing creditor or create a federal “super-creditor.” Nordic Village, invoked by Roberts and Alito, reinforces that we require an unequivocal statement to expand the Government’s exposure; reading § 106(a) to alter § 544(b)(1)’s substantive scope would extend the waiver by implication. Under a strict textualist/originalist approach, any remedial gap is for Congress to fix explicitly, not for us to cure by deeming away § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor requirement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “hollowing out” argument has intuitive force, but under the clear-statement rule for sovereign-immunity waivers it cannot justify reading § 106(a) to alter § 544(b)(1)’s substantive, derivative predicate that an actual unsecured creditor “may avoid” the transfer under nonbankruptcy applicable law. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 106(a) can still do real work by removing immunity as a defense in properly constituted § 544 actions where a qualifying creditor exists (or where applicable law itself permits suit), without converting § 544(b)(1) into a hypothetical-creditor device whenever the United States is the transferee. Nordic Village, cited by multiple colleagues, reinforces that we do not extend waivers by implication to expand liability or dispense with statutory conditions, and Sotomayor’s reading would effectively do both. The practical concern that some transfers to the United States remain unavoidable under § 544(b)(1) is for Congress to address expressly, not for us to cure by rewriting the derivative structure Congress chose.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan make the best textual point that § 544(b)(1) is framed as derivative and speaks in terms of what a real creditor “may avoid” under applicable law, and Nordic Village cautions against expanding waivers by implication. But their construction still lets sovereign immunity re-enter through § 544’s incorporated state-law cause of action, leaving § 106(a)’s explicit waiver “with respect to” § 544 doing vanishingly little precisely in the cases Congress would most plausibly have had in mind when it singled § 544 out by name. Under my pragmatic, consequence-attentive approach, I read “with respect to” to waive immunity for the full § 544(b)(1) mechanism as it operates in practice (derivative state-law avoidance), rather than treating the actual-creditor requirement as an immunity trap that defeats equitable recovery for the bankruptcy estate. Nordic Village still matters, but Congress responded with a provision-by-provision waiver; I do not think strict construction requires us to render that targeted waiver largely ineffectual in the very setting where immunity would otherwise block avoidance.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Congress’s decision to list § 544 in § 106(a) suggests it wanted the waiver to matter in the very derivative actions trustees typically bring, and we should not read the waiver to be purely ornamental. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, § 544(b)(1) is not just a venue for an “immunity defense”; it defines the trustee’s power by incorporating a real creditor’s ability to avoid under applicable law, and § 106(a) waives immunity without unmistakably altering that incorporated predicate. Nordic Village’s strict-construction principle therefore cuts against treating “with respect to” as a quiet conversion of § 544(b)(1) into a hypothetical-creditor mechanism whenever the United States is the transferee. On my pragmatic textualism, the administrable middle ground is to give § 106(a) effect where a qualifying creditor exists, but not to deem one into existence by implication when sovereign immunity means none “may avoid” outside bankruptcy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s “hollow waiver” argument has intuitive force, but it treats § 106(a) as silently revising § 544(b)(1)’s substantive, derivative trigger—“a creditor … may avoid”—into a hypothetical-creditor regime whenever the United States is the transferee. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 106(a) can still do meaningful work by removing immunity as a defense in properly constituted § 544 actions where a qualifying creditor exists under applicable law; it need not (and under Nordic Village cannot) be read to supply a missing state-law cause of action against the sovereign. The phrase “with respect to” is not the unmistakable clear statement needed to expand liability beyond § 544(b)(1)’s built-in limitation, and separation-of-powers concerns counsel against our creating a federal “super-creditor” by inference rather than legislation. Accordingly, I remain with the Petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point remains that reading § 106(a) narrowly risks making the waiver “with respect to” § 544 ineffective in the very scenario where the United States is the transferee, but that argument treats § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor requirement as merely an immunity obstacle rather than a substantive condition on the trustee’s power. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 544(b)(1) incorporates state-law avoiding rights only to the extent an actual unsecured creditor “may avoid” the transfer under applicable law; when sovereign immunity means no creditor can sue the United States outside bankruptcy, the statutory predicate never arises, and § 106(a) cannot be read to supply a missing cause of action without an unequivocal statement. Nordic Village’s strict-construction rule confirms that we should not extend a waiver from removing a defense into effectively creating a “super-creditor” federal power untethered to real-world creditor rights. I therefore remain with the Petitioner because this interpretation preserves § 544(b)(1)’s historically derivative design while still giving § 106(a) operative effect where a qualifying creditor exists.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s hollow-waiver point is the best pushback: if § 106(a) waives immunity “with respect to” § 544, it seems odd to let immunity defeat the archetypal § 544(b)(1) action whenever the United States is the transferee. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 544(b)(1) is not merely an immunity “obstacle”; it is a derivative grant that turns on whether an actual unsecured creditor “may avoid” the transfer under applicable nonbankruptcy law, and federal sovereign immunity means no such creditor exists here. Under Nordic Village’s clear-statement rule, § 106(a)’s waiver cannot be read to silently supply that missing predicate or to create substantive state-law avoidance exposure against the United States by implication. This construction still gives § 106(a) work to do in § 544 cases where a qualifying creditor exists under applicable law, while preserving § 544(b)(1)’s text and derivative design.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to worry that a narrow reading can make § 106(a)’s waiver feel functionally thin in the very § 544(b)(1) cases trustees often bring, but that pragmatic concern cannot override the clear-statement rule for sovereign-immunity waivers or justify treating § 106(a) as silently rewriting § 544(b)(1)’s substantive trigger. As the Chief and Justice Kagan emphasize, § 544(b)(1) is expressly derivative—its power exists only if an actual unsecured creditor “may avoid” the transfer under applicable nonbankruptcy law—and § 106(a)’s “with respect to” language most naturally operates to remove an immunity defense in a properly triggered § 544 action, not to conjure a qualifying creditor where none could sue the United States outside bankruptcy. Nordic Village reinforces that we do not expand governmental exposure or dispense with statutory conditions by implication, and the trustee’s reading would effectively create a federal “super-creditor” untethered to real-world creditor rights. On a progressive pragmatic view, the more procedurally fair and administrable line is to keep § 544(b)(1) anchored to actual creditor entitlements and leave any broader exposure of the United States in this setting for Congress to state unmistakably.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is written as a derivative power: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if an actual unsecured creditor “may avoid” it under “applicable law,” and here no creditor could bring the requisite state-law fraudulent-transfer action against the United States outside bankruptcy because sovereign immunity would bar it. Section 106(a) waives sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-based predicate; it merely removes an immunity defense once the trustee otherwise satisfies § 544’s terms. Under the strict-construction rule for waivers of federal sovereign immunity, any plausible reading that preserves immunity must control, and Nordic Village underscores that waivers must be unequivocally expressed and not implied to expand substantive liability beyond the statute’s conditions. A narrow holding for the government preserves § 544(b)(1)’s established derivative structure and avoids an atextual expansion that could unsettle bankruptcy-federalism balances by effectively creating new causes of action against the United States via state law.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if “an unsecured creditor” could avoid it under “applicable law,” and where federal sovereign immunity would bar every such creditor from suing the United States outside bankruptcy, the statutory predicate is missing. Section 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 removes the Government’s immunity defense only for actions that otherwise satisfy § 544(b)(1); it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s actual-creditor requirement into a hypothetical-creditor rule. This reading accords with the clear-statement rule for waivers of sovereign immunity and the instruction to construe such waivers strictly, see United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992), and avoids inferring an expansion of substantive avoidance power beyond the text. Because Congress did not unmistakably state that § 106(a) dispenses with § 544(b)(1)’s real-world creditor requirement, the trustee cannot use state law to claw back tax payments from the United States in these circumstances.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if there exists an actual unsecured creditor who “may” avoid it under “applicable law” outside bankruptcy, and here sovereign immunity means no real-world creditor could bring the requisite state-law fraudulent-transfer action against the United States. Section 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 removes an immunity defense to a properly grounded § 544 action, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s predicate creditor requirement or create a cause of action where no creditor could sue in the first place. Under the clear-statement rule, waivers of sovereign immunity are strictly construed and cannot be extended by implication to expand substantive liability beyond the statute’s terms. Practical consequences also counsel against the respondent’s reading, which would allow trustees to leverage state law to claw back federal tax payments in bankruptcy even though Congress did not clearly authorize that result.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 106(a) unambiguously waives federal sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544, and that waiver should be read to allow the trustee to pursue the same § 544(b)(1) avoidance action against the United States that would otherwise exist against a private transferee, rather than letting immunity silently re-enter through § 544(b)(1)’s derivative framing. While Nordic Village requires waivers be “unequivocally expressed” and strictly construed, Congress responded by enacting § 106(a)’s express waiver as to specified Code provisions, including § 544, and that text is best understood to remove the very immunity obstacle that would otherwise defeat the action. A contrary reading would hollow out § 106(a) in a core bankruptcy context and frustrate equitable recovery for creditors—often including workers, tort victims, and other vulnerable claimants—by insulating tax payments from fraudulent-transfer scrutiny solely because the transferee is the government. Consistent with bankruptcy’s remedial purpose and § 106(a)’s plain language, I would hold the trustee may proceed under § 544(b)(1) notwithstanding that sovereign immunity would block the same suit outside bankruptcy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if an actual unsecured creditor "may avoid" it under "applicable law" outside bankruptcy, and here federal sovereign immunity would bar any such state-law suit against the United States, leaving no qualifying triggering creditor. Section 106(a) waives sovereign immunity "with respect to" § 544, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s predicate requirement; it removes an immunity defense once a trustee has a valid § 544(b)(1) claim rather than supplying a creditor who could sue in the real world. Reading § 106(a) to eliminate the actual-creditor condition would expand § 544(b)(1) beyond its coherent statutory design and collide with the clear-statement/strict-construction approach to sovereign-immunity waivers reflected in Nordic Village. A workable, middle-ground reading preserves § 106(a)’s waiver for § 544 actions where a creditor exists under applicable law, while respecting § 544(b)(1)’s built-in limits when sovereign immunity prevents any creditor from suing the United States outside bankruptcy.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is written in unmistakably derivative terms: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if “a creditor holding an unsecured claim” could avoid it “under applicable law,” and where the transferee is the United States no real-world creditor could bring the state-law action because sovereign immunity bars it. Section 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 is best read to remove an immunity defense once a trustee has a valid § 544(b)(1) cause of action; it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-based predicate or create a federal “super-creditor” untethered from any creditor’s actual outside-bankruptcy rights, consistent with separation-of-powers and the statute’s plain text. Under Nordic Village, waivers of federal sovereign immunity must be “unequivocally expressed” and construed strictly in the sovereign’s favor; at minimum, it is plausible that § 106(a) does not eliminate § 544(b)(1)’s requirement of an actual creditor who could sue under nonbankruptcy law, so the trustee’s claim fails. Reading § 106(a) to silently expand § 544(b)(1) would exceed what Congress clearly said and would effectively let bankruptcy courts displace the sovereign-immunity baseline without a clear statement tied to the underlying “applicable law.”

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if an actual unsecured creditor could have avoided it under “applicable law,” and here no such creditor exists because federal sovereign immunity would bar any state-law fraudulent-transfer suit against the United States outside bankruptcy. Section 106(a)’s waiver of sovereign immunity “with respect to” § 544 removes an immunity defense to a properly grounded § 544 action, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-based predicate or create a cause of action where none exists in the real world. Under this Court’s strict-construction approach to waivers of sovereign immunity, as emphasized in Nordic Village, a waiver must be unequivocally expressed and should not be read to alter substantive conditions Congress separately imposed in § 544(b)(1). This reading also preserves workability and predictability by keeping § 544(b)(1) tethered to an identifiable actual creditor, rather than making the trustee’s power turn on hypothetical creditors divested only of immunity obstacles.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: the trustee may avoid a transfer only if there exists an actual unsecured creditor who “may avoid” it under “applicable law” outside bankruptcy, and sovereign immunity means no such creditor could sue the United States under state fraudulent-transfer law in the real world. Section 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 removes the Government’s immunity as a defense in bankruptcy proceedings, but it does not rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s predicate condition by creating a creditor cause of action that cannot exist outside bankruptcy. Reading § 106(a) to supply the missing “actual creditor” would extend the waiver beyond what Congress “unequivocally expressed,” contrary to the rule that waivers of federal sovereign immunity must be clear and strictly construed. See United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30 (1992).

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 544(b)(1) is textually derivative: it authorizes avoidance only of a transfer that is “voidable under applicable law by a creditor,” which requires an actual, real-world unsecured creditor who could bring the state-law fraudulent-transfer action outside bankruptcy. Because federal sovereign immunity would bar any such creditor from suing the United States under state law, the trustee cannot satisfy § 544(b)(1)’s predicate, and § 106(a)’s waiver “with respect to” § 544 cannot be read to rewrite § 544(b)(1)’s creditor-based condition rather than merely removing an immunity defense once that condition is met. This reading accords with the clear-statement rule that waivers must be “unequivocally expressed” and “construed strictly in favor of the sovereign,” and where a plausible interpretation preserves immunity courts must adopt it. See United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 503 U.S. 30, 34 (1992).
